title: Supporting the Uptake of Evidence‐Based Care for Degenerative Meniscal Tears and Early Knee Osteoarthritis: A Collaborative Approach to the Development of an Intervention Using Stakeholder Perspectives and Integrating Behaviour Change Theory

paragraphs.en: The burden of knee pain on healthcare resources is increasing [1]. Approximately one in five of all consultations in general practice are musculoskeletal, with the knee being the most common presentation after the lower back [2]. Knee pain also accounts for the greatest number of new consultations seen in Irish secondary care orthopaedic clinics, where meniscal pathology is the most frequent diagnosis after osteoarthritis (OA) [3]. Meniscal pathology in middle‐aged and older adults is usually degenerative, marked by slow progression of the lesion [4]. A degenerative meniscal tear (DMT) in a symptomatic knee is synonymous with early osteoarthritic changes and typically exists in the context of articular cartilage degradation and other early degenerative changes [5, 6]. No clinical tests or symptoms reliably distinguish the two entities, and both symptomatic early‐stage knee OA and a DMT typically present with intermittent, activity‐induced knee pain, with limited or no radiographic changes [7, 8, 9, 10].

Treatment recommendations for DMT and early OA advise a clinical diagnosis without imaging, and conservative management through patient education, exercise therapy and lifestyle change promoting weight management and physical activity [11, 12, 13]. This approach is associated with reduced pain and improved function and quality of life across multiple healthcare settings [14, 15, 16, 17].

Imaging findings have limited relevance to management in early‐stage knee OA [7, 18]. Despite this, inappropriate use of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to investigate knee pain in middle‐aged and older adults, without a history of trauma or red flags, is well documented, both in Ireland and internationally [19, 20, 21, 22], and continues to rise [23]. Overuse of diagnostic imaging has been implicated in driving patients with DMT, and their healthcare professionals (HCPs), to seek early orthopaedic or surgical solutions [24, 25, 26], and has been implicated in persistently high knee arthroscopy rates in some countries [26, 27]. Arthroscopic surgery, or partial meniscectomy, as a treatment of DMT is no more effective than sham surgery for improving pain and reducing disability [28, 29], and several studies have associated this procedure with a higher risk of OA progression [30, 31, 32]. Importantly, continued use of ‘unnecessary interventions’ for knee OA, such as MRI and arthroscopy, does not appear to translate into better clinical outcomes [23, 33] and their overuse has important resource implications, further underscoring the need to reduce mismanagement and low‐value care [34, 35].

Meanwhile, there is sub‐optimal use of recommended care for DMT and early OA. The core treatments of education, exercise and weight management are under‐prescribed for knee OA, and there is a low uptake by patients [36, 37, 38, 39, 40]. A substantial proportion of patients with knee OA referred for orthopaedic opinion have not adequately trialled first‐line care, including exercise therapy [41, 42]. Qualitative research with people diagnosed with DMTs and HCPs underscores these findings. GPs and patients describe bypassing first‐line conservative care, such as physiotherapy, in favour of a surgical opinion [24, 25, 43]. Physiotherapists also described a pattern of care that involved unwarranted imaging and early referral to orthopaedic specialists [44].

To bridge the evidence–practice gap, there is a need to identify the HCP, patient and health service barriers to recommended care and address these with a multi‐level intervention. A recent systematic review of the implementation of OA management programmes in primary and community care identified barriers and enablers across individual, service and health‐system levels, including factors related to HCP's knowledge and skills, patient beliefs and capabilities, and limited public funding and workforce [45]. These findings reinforce the need for implementation strategies that address determinants of care at multiple levels rather than focusing solely on professional knowledge or behaviour. The National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) and the Medical Research Council (MRC) recommend that such complex interventions should be grounded in the theoretical basis of behavioural change and respond to underlying behavioural and contextual determinants [46].

Several studies have used theory‐driven approaches in designing interventions to better align knee OA care with best‐practice recommendations by improving the delivery of first‐line care or optimising referral pathways [47, 48, 49, 50]. However, a scoping review of existing models and interventions to improve delivery of non‐surgical OA management in primary care identified important limitations, including insufficient integration of implementation and behavioural change theory and limited stakeholder involvement in intervention development [51].

Another criticism of the existing interventions is their reliance on a ‘one size fits all’ approach despite the highly heterogeneous clinical knee OA population [51]. There is increasing recognition of the importance of focusing on individuals with early symptomatic knee OA and intervening at an earlier stage of disease. This reflects the concept of a ‘window of opportunity’ in early knee OA [8], particularly given evidence that a new diagnosis of knee OA is strongly associated with subsequently developing a range of new comorbidities and functional impairments [52]. To date, most interventions developed to improve evidence‐based care for knee OA have focused on people with an established diagnosis of OA and have typically included both hip and knee OA [47, 53, 54], limiting their applicability to early disease.

While the strong recommendations against surgery for degenerative meniscal pathology are gradually translating to practice [55, 56, 57], uncertainty remains regarding how best to implement conservative management, particularly for people with DMT and early OA. Recent evidence indicates that implementation of recommended OA care is influenced by interacting barriers at patient, HCP, service and health‐system levels [45, 58]. To our knowledge, no theory‐informed intervention with stakeholder involvement has been developed that specifically targets people with DMT and early OA changes and/or their healthcare providers. This study aims to describe the systematic development of a multifaceted implementation intervention to improve the delivery and uptake of evidence‐based care for people with DMTs and early knee OA.

We used a four‐step approach, consisting of guiding questions, first described by French et al., to structure the intervention development process (Figure 1) [59]. This approach combines behavioural change theory, stakeholder involvement and evidence on intervention effectiveness. For further guidance, we also drew on case examples that outlined their use of this four‐step development process [49, 60]. The process is reported in line with the Guidance for the Reporting of Intervention Development (GUIDED) checklist [61]. The Guidance for Reporting Involvement of Patients and the Public (GRIPP) 2 short form (SF) reporting guideline checklist [62] was also followed. Both reporting guidelines are presented in Supplementary File 1. The research team provided expertise in knee OA, general practice, orthopaedics, qualitative, health services research and designing behavioural theory informed interventions to the development process.

This intervention development study is part of the Knowledge translation and Exercise for Degenerative Meniscal Pathology and Early osteoarthritis (KNEE‐DEeP) project, which builds on earlier studies [25, 43, 44], with plans to test the intervention in a future KNEE‐DEeP feasibility study [63]. The project is set in the Southwest region of Ireland, where people with knee pain access a mixed public–private system of healthcare. The number of people paying for private health insurance is substantial, estimated to be 48% of the population. Publicly funded physiotherapy is delivered by the Health Services Executive (HSE), but long waiting times can hinder access, and not all patients are entitled to this service [64]. Approximately 42% of the Irish population has access to free GP care [65]. Patients without entitlement to public physiotherapy or free GP care pay out‐of‐pocket [66].

Stakeholder consultation is a key component of intervention development, ensuring interventions are acceptable, engaging and feasible prior to piloting [67, 68]. This is particularly important for DMT and early OA, where the evidence base for implementing non‐surgical care remains limited. Stakeholders included HCPs and people with lived experience (PwLE) of DMT and/or early knee OA. All stakeholders were distinct from participants in the baseline qualitative studies.

sections.title: Stakeholders With Lived Experience of Knee Pain

paragraphs.en: A panel of six PwLE of DMT/early OA were recruited from the Southwest using an information flyer distributed through physiotherapy clinics and social media. These middle‐aged and older adults represented a spectrum of people with degenerative knee disease who had sought care from the primary and secondary healthcare services in Ireland. Two stakeholders had previously undergone arthroscopy, three had early OA changes or a diagnosis of a DMT and one had established OA.

These stakeholders, including six general practitioners (GPs) based in the Southwest of Ireland and six physiotherapists working in public musculoskeletal services, were recruited through professional networks. In addition, two orthopaedic surgeons from public hospitals and one health service (physiotherapy) manager were consulted.

Stakeholder consultation occurred across the intervention development process. Stakeholder groups were consulted separately to acknowledge potential power dynamics and to facilitate in‐depth discussion within each group. Three in‐person meetings were held with PwLE at early, middle and late stages to inform and refine the intervention. GP input on intervention development was obtained during a group online meeting hosted on Microsoft Teams. During a separate 1‐h meeting, held in‐person, input was sought on intervention feasibility and acceptability from the group of physiotherapist stakeholders. Additional feedback from a subset of these GP and physiotherapist stakeholders was collected via email during finalisation of the intervention. Two orthopaedic surgeons and a health service manager also provided feedback on intervention feasibility and acceptability during one‐to‐one in‐person meetings.

Stakeholder perspectives were considered iteratively at each stage of intervention development by the researchers, when stakeholder groups were invited to consider various aspects of the intervention (e.g., proposed target behaviours, identified barriers and enablers, and draft intervention components). No formal consensus methods were used, and there was no pre‐defined threshold for stakeholder agreement. Areas of agreement and disagreement within and across the different stakeholder groups were identified and discussed by the research team and considered alongside the evidence, behavioural theory and local feasibility.

All consultations were facilitated by a practising physiotherapist and member of the research team (H.O.L). Stakeholders provided written informed consent for audio‐recording of consultation meetings and the use of anonymised extracts. Meeting transcripts were analysed using qualitative content analysis to extract and organise stakeholder feedback that informs the intervention development process. Relevant sections of each transcript were identified and coded according to their content and relevance to intervention development. Codes were grouped into broader categories representing the issues raised by stakeholders. The analysis focused on stakeholder views regarding: (i) the relevance and acceptability of proposed target behaviours; (ii) perceived barriers and enablers to the target behaviours; (iii) preferences for how barriers and enablers could be addressed; (iv) the acceptability, feasibility and practicability of proposed intervention components and modes of delivery; and (v) suggested modifications to proposed intervention content or delivery. Stakeholder groups were considered separately to preserve the perspectives of different groups. Analysis remained primarily focused on the practical implications of stakeholder feedback for intervention development. Findings were summarised for consideration by the research team and used to inform the next step of the intervention development process. Ethical approval for stakeholder consultation was granted by the University of Limerick Faculty of Education and Health Science Research Ethics Committee on 16 February 2023 (Project ID: 2023_02_20_EHS).

sections.title: Applying a Stepwise Approach to Intervention Development

paragraphs.en: The approach by French et al. [59] is outlined in the following four steps.

sections.title: Step 1: Who Needs to Do What, Differently?

paragraphs.en: Delivering evidence‐based care for DMT and early knee OA requires HCP and patient behaviours to align with best‐practice guidelines. Our focus was on the provision and uptake of core recommended treatments, namely education and exercise, while reducing the use of low‐value care such as inappropriate imaging and referral to secondary care, without first trialling core treatments. Deviations from best practice guidelines were identified through review of the Irish and international DMT and OA literature describing current practice and behaviours [25, 37, 43, 44, 69]. We augmented this with other relevant studies from the knee OA and DMT literature [24, 36, 40].

In the initial stage, input from GP and PwLE stakeholders helped refine the target behaviours. At the first in‐person meeting, PwLE shared their previous experiences of seeking care and features of an ideal consultation for knee pain. GPs offered suggestions at their online meeting to improve current care and identified behaviours that would be pragmatic and feasible within routine consultations.

sections.title: Step 2: Using a Theoretical Framework, Which Barriers and Enablers Need to Be Addressed?

paragraphs.en: To identify specific targets for behaviour change, we applied the refined Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) (V.2) to explore barriers and enablers to the implementation of recommended behaviours by GPs and patients [70]. The refined TDF comprises 14 domains (Knowledge, Skills, Memory, Attention, and Decision Processes, Behavioural Regulation, Environmental Context and Resources, Social Influences, Beliefs About Capabilities, Social/Professional Role and Identity, Beliefs About Consequences, Emotions, Goals, Intentions, Reinforcement, and Optimism/Pessimism) that influence behaviour and has been effectively used in musculoskeletal research to identify behavioural determinants [49, 71]. Beyond providing a detailed understanding of target behaviours, the TDF also supports the selection of appropriate strategies and techniques aimed at modifying clinical behaviours and improving clinical practice [72, 73].

To understand which barriers and enablers needed to be addressed, we primarily drew on previously conducted qualitative studies with GPs, physiotherapists and individuals with DMT, completed by members of the research team [25, 43, 44]. The analysis was informed by the TDF domain definitions, which were used within a deductive framework to organise barriers and enablers relevant to the target behaviours.

For the GP perspective, qualitative interview data from 17 GPs exploring their management of DMTs were re‐analysed to explore why evidence‐based behaviours were not routinely enacted in clinical practice. The methods and primary findings from this study are reported in detail elsewhere [43]. To understand the perspectives of PwLE, previously collected interview data from 11 individuals with knee pain attributed to DMT, which explored their treatment experiences and expectations, were also re‐analysed [25]. These datasets were selected for secondary analysis because they contained rich accounts from the key participant groups relevant to the target behaviours and participants with direct experience of delivering or receiving care for DMT or early OA within the context of the Irish health service. Although existing literature provides a broader evidence base regarding barriers and enablers to recommended OA care, the selected datasets offered an opportunity to examine these determinants specifically within the target population and healthcare context of the proposed intervention. Sample sizes were determined in the primary studies and were not recalculated for the secondary analysis. Instead, all transcripts from the selected primary studies were reviewed, and each manuscript was found to contain excerpts relevant to the target behaviours, and these were included in the analysis.

For this secondary analysis, a hybrid inductive–deductive approach to qualitative analysis was employed [74]. First, two researchers (H.O.L. and K.M.C.) independently reviewed a subset of transcripts and coded data relevant to the target behaviours. The researchers compared their coding and discussed discrepancies to refine the interpretation and develop an agreed coding framework. A third researcher (K.R.) was available to resolve disagreements if required but was not needed. The resulting coding framework was then applied by H.O.L. to all relevant transcripts, using NVivo 12 to manage the data. Having inductively assigned codes to the data, next the identified codes were deductively mapped to the relevant domains of the refined TDF independently by two authors (H.O.L. and K.M.C.) [75], with discrepancies discussed until consensus was achieved. Barriers and enablers for each target behaviour were subsequently identified within each relevant TDF domain.

TDF domains were considered prominent when they were directly relevant to the target behaviour, expressed by multiple participants, and judged to be likely to influence the target behaviours. Barriers and enablers were prioritised if they were frequently identified and considered potentially modifiable. A subsequent discussion with the core research team (H.O.L., K.M.C., L.R., L.M., C.T. and H.F.) refined and confirmed the TDF domains and determinants. This discussion focused on stakeholder feedback, implications for intervention development within the health service context and the wider OA literature.

At a second in‐person meeting, PwLE were presented with and discussed a lay summary of the identified barriers and enablers derived from the secondary qualitative data analysis. GP stakeholders were similarly presented with and discussed a summary of the TDF‐informed analysis during their online meeting. Feedback from both stakeholder groups was used in discussions with the core research team to identify which barriers were considered most modifiable and to build consensus on how these could be broadly addressed within the intervention.

sections.title: Step 3: Which Intervention Components (BCTs and Mode(s) of Delivery) Could Overcome the Modifiable Barriers and Enhance the Enablers?

paragraphs.en: Mapping TDF domains to appropriate BCTs

A behaviour change technique (BCT) is defined as an observable and replicable component designed to change behaviour [76]. For this step, barriers and enablers, categorised by TDF domains, were linked to appropriate BCTs using the Theory and Techniques Tool (available at https://theoryandtechniquetool.humanbehaviourchange.org/tool). This tool maps 74 BCTs from the BCT Taxonomy (BCTTv1) [73], to their corresponding mechanisms of action in the TDF, and indicates the strength of association based on data from a literature synthesis and an expert consensus study [77]. Two research team members (H.O.L. and K.M.C.) met to create an initial list of BCTs. This selection focused on BCTs that had the strongest evidence according to the Theory and Technique Tool. This initial list was narrowed down by the researchers using stakeholder recommendations on how to address the target behaviours, gathered during Step 2 consultations and what was considered feasible within the scope of the current study.
Developing intervention components and combining them into an acceptable and deliverable intervention

Next, we operationalised or transformed shortlisted BCTs into potential intervention content (what will actually be delivered) and identified possible modes of delivery (how each BCT would be delivered). Whilst evidence relating specifically to implementing DMT clinical recommendations is lacking, we considered evidence on the effectiveness of implementation strategies in OA or musculoskeletal care [78, 79]. Discussion among the core research team on what was pragmatic and feasible within the project scope was used to arrive at a consensus on a draft implementation intervention that incorporated operationalised BCTs with proposed modes of delivery.

At the third in‐person meeting, PwLE were presented with the draft intervention, in which several operationalised BCTs were combined into separate intervention components. PwLE were facilitated to discuss the acceptability and practicability of proposed intervention components and how they would work within the local context. Input was also sought on an early draft of an educational leaflet for patients, which integrated responses to information needs identified by PwLE at earlier stakeholder meetings.

Three GPs who had previously participated in the Step 2 online stakeholder meeting provided feedback on the feasibility and acceptability of the draft intervention via email, with particular focus on the components targeting GPs. Six physiotherapists were consulted at this stage through an in‐person meeting, where perspectives were sought on the acceptability and feasibility of the draft intervention, particularly regarding components proposed for delivery by physiotherapists. Two orthopaedic consultants were provided with an overview of the intervention development process and asked to give individual feedback on the acceptability and feasibility of the proposed intervention.

sections.title: Decision on Final Intervention Using APEASE Criteria

paragraphs.en: The core research team met to finalise the intervention content, guided by the APEASE (affordability, practicability, effectiveness, acceptability, side effects and equity) criteria [80]. This framework assists researchers in the later stages of intervention development to assess intervention acceptability and feasibility in a thorough and methodical way [80]. PwLE, GP, physiotherapist and orthopaedic consultant stakeholder feedback informed what was acceptable, practical and equitable. We also considered what was feasible to evaluate within a pilot study and routine practice. For effectiveness, we reviewed any evidence from the OA and musculoskeletal literature that supported the shortlisted components. Affordability and sustainability were assessed in the context of Irish public healthcare resources, with input from the manager of the local publicly funded physiotherapy service.

Training materials for HCPs and patient educational resources created by two team members (H.O.L. and K.M.C.) to accompany the final intervention were circulated by email to a subset of GP, physiotherapist and PwLE stakeholders. Their feedback was used to further refine and finalise these resources.

sections.title: Step 4. How Can Behaviour Change Be Measured and Understood?

paragraphs.en: In this step, a theory‐informed logic model was developed by the research team representing the programme theory of the intervention. The ‘active ingredients’ of the intervention were specified using BCTs, with hypothesised mechanisms of action used to describe the processes through which these techniques were expected to influence professional and patient behaviour [77, 81]. We also outlined outcome measures designed to capture change in GP and patient behaviour in a future feasibility study set within the context of the Irish health service. This approach was guided by literature on programme theory [82, 83] and the MRC framework for developing and evaluating complex interventions [46, 84, 85].

sections.title: Step 1: Identify Who Needs to Do What, Differently

paragraphs.en: The target behaviours for this intervention were informed by international guidelines and clinical practice recommendations for the management of knee OA and DMTs, which recommend clinical diagnosis without routine imaging [11, 22, 86, 87] and provision of first‐line treatments (education and structured exercise therapy) [11, 13], and strongly advise against arthroscopic partial meniscectomy [11, 12].

Evidence indicates persistent suboptimal provision and uptake of recommended care for DMT and knee OA [25, 36, 37, 40, 44, 51, 88] alongside continued use of unnecessary low‐value interventions such as MRI and arthroscopy [20, 21, 22, 23]. As change is needed at both the HCP and patient level and as GPs in Ireland act as gatekeepers to specialist referral and publicly funded diagnostic imaging [89], GPs were selected as the primary target HCPs for the intervention.

sections.title: Integrating Stakeholder Feedback on Target Behaviours

paragraphs.en: Consultation with GP stakeholders highlighted the importance for GPs of protecting their professional autonomy and flexibility to address each patient presentation individually. Accordingly, rather than mandating GPs to avoid specific clinical behaviours (e.g., imaging or secondary care referral), it was considered more acceptable and pragmatic to advise delaying non‐recommended care, at least until patients were provided with a self‐management and exercise programme. Other proposed target behaviours were that GPs would provide patients with a brief exercise recommendation and a brief clinical assessment during the consultation. GP stakeholders supported this, with the understanding that onward referral to physiotherapy would facilitate more comprehensive assessment and tailored exercise prescription.

PwLE also provided feedback on the proposed target behaviours at their first meeting. While views varied regarding the role of imaging in early management, there was general agreement that deferring imaging, particularly MRI, until after provision of an exercise and self‐management programme was acceptable. Patients emphasised the importance of receiving a diagnosis and explanation of symptoms but agreed that a thorough clinical assessment could help meet their need for symptom explanation and validation.
Three target behaviours for GPs and one patient target behaviour are specified in Table 1 by describing who, what, when, where and how often each behaviour is to be performed.

sections.title: Step 2: Identify the Barriers and Enablers That Need to Be Addressed Using a Theoretical Framework
Barriers and Enablers to GP Target Behaviours

paragraphs.en: From the 17 qualitative interviews with GPs, we identified the following 10 TDF domains that prominently influenced the GP target behaviours: knowledge, skills, beliefs about capabilities, environmental context and resources, emotion, motivation, beliefs about consequences, professional role and identity, social influences, memory, attention and decision‐making processes (Table 2).

Barriers to Target Behaviour 1 (conducts a clinical assessment and provides a diagnosis) included fear of misdiagnosis, low confidence in musculoskeletal skills and competing priorities in a time‐pressurised consultation, which represented a combination of cognitive, emotional and contextual influences as described by the TDF.

Barriers to Target Behaviour 2 (avoids/defers imaging and referral to secondary care) included managing patient expectations, desire for a specialist opinion (e.g., orthopaedic) and lack of access to other management options such as physiotherapy. Enablers of this target behaviour were GPs' awareness of the negative implications of unnecessary imaging and the leveraging of existing patient relationships to help manage patient expectations.

For Target Behaviour 3 (provision of education and exercise), GPs' perception of their professional role, perceived patient disinterest, GPs' knowledge and skills, and lack of access to physiotherapy and trustworthy patient educational resources were all cited as barriers. Enablers of this behaviour include GPs' motivation to promote physical activity with their patients and frustration with current management options.

sections.title: Barriers and Enablers to Patient Target Behaviour

paragraphs.en: The integration of qualitative data from 11 patient interviews identified barriers and enablers that corresponded to 10 TDF domains (beliefs about consequences, intention, behavioural regulation, motivation, knowledge, belief about capabilities, emotion, social influences, environmental context and resources, and reinforcement) (Table 3).

Barriers to patient engagement with exercise therapy and self‐management of their knee pain included a lack of knowledge, confidence and fear of doing harm with exercise, negative expectations of conservative management and the perception of surgery as a more straightforward solution. Reinforcement of beliefs about the need for imaging or surgery by others and lack of access to evidence‐based physiotherapy were other barriers to patients engaging with exercise therapy. Enablers included patients' positive past experiences with exercise and their desire to return to valued activities.

sections.title: Step 3: Which Intervention Components (BCTs and Mode(s) of Delivery) Could Overcome the Modifiable Barriers and Enhance the Enablers?

paragraphs.en: Identify potential behavioural change techniques and modes of delivery to overcome barriers and enhance the enablers

The initial longlist of BCTs mapped to each relevant domain for GPs and patient target behaviours is displayed in Supplementary File 2: Tables A and B. A summary of the rationale for excluding BCTs is summarised in Supplementary File 2: Tables C and D.
Identify what is likely to be feasible, locally relevant and acceptable and combine identified components into an acceptable intervention that can be delivered
The draft intervention, incorporating shortlisted and operationalised BCTs (italicised), stakeholder feedback, and evidence from relevant literature, is outlined below.

In musculoskeletal care implementation research, multi‐facet component interventions are more effective than single‐component interventions at changing health professionals' clinical behaviours [79]. Interventions that have demonstrated a small but positive effect on clinical behaviours include dissemination of clinical practice guidelines, interactive educational meetings, monitoring the performance of healthcare delivery, peer assessment, and use of local opinion leaders [79, 90].

Interventions to enhance the initial GP–patient consultation that typically involves education and training of the provider (GP) have demonstrated improved uptake of evidence‐based care [50, 91] and, in some instances, reduced low‐value healthcare usage [92], although evidence of improved clinical outcomes compared to usual care is mixed [51]. Such approaches frequently encompass a tailored care plan, delivered by another member of the multi‐disciplinary team [48, 50]. Based on this evidence, our intervention proposed a similar model, with the physiotherapist tailoring a plan to support patients with behavioural change and self‐management.

Interactive educational workshops for clinicians have enhanced evidence‐based clinical behaviours for low back pain and reduced low‐value imaging [78, 93] and improved the uptake of core recommended treatments among patients with OA [94]. For workshop content, GP stakeholders expressed interest in understanding the evidence base for management of DMTs and knee OA (information provision, information about health consequences and credible source), alongside acquiring practical assessment and communication skills (rehearsal of relevant skills, instruction on how to perform a behaviour, and demonstration of a behaviour). One GP noted:
I think if we have a real good spiel on how to explain or an explanation on when to do an MRI and when not to, that's something that's very helpful
GP Stakeholder 3

In addition to revising practical assessment skills, GPs agreed that a laminated Quick Reference Guide for their consultation room would help aid diagnosis (conserving mental resource and adding objects to the environment). GPs favoured methods to deliver patient education that were quick, simple and therefore likely to be feasible in routine practice.
If you are going to provide something for GPs, it must be, you know, probably no more than three points. “Here is what you say.”
GP Stakeholder 1

In response, four key patient education messages for verbal delivery by GPs were identified to support efficient education (information provision and credible source). These messages addressed common patient misconceptions and unhelpful beliefs identified in the OA and DMT qualitative data [25, 43, 95]. Supportive, evidence‐based educational messages within ‘enhanced’ GP consultations have improved concordance with low back pain and OA guideline recommendations [96, 97]. PwLE stakeholders emphasised the importance of having this verbal information backed up in a written format (adding objects to the environment).
It's having that key information in front of you, and for me personally, I think it has to be in writing.
PwLE Stakeholder 2

Both GP and PwLE stakeholder groups requested a Patient Advice Leaflet containing educational information written in lay language and should include the credentials of the researchers who compiled the information and the project funder (credible source). To support exercise provision, GPs requested a simple ‘starter’ for inclusion in the Patient Advice Leaflet, with images and links to videos (instructions on how to perform behaviour).
But it would be really nice to have something very quick that you could kind of get them (the patient) started with.
GP Stakeholder 5

The suggestion of a GP follow‐up appointment by PwLE stakeholders was deemed unfeasible by GPs due to time constraints. Instead, it was agreed that a management plan be documented on the Patient Advice Leaflet and include a planned GP follow‐up appointment if necessary.
Several GP stakeholders reiterated the challenge of prioritising knee pain within a multimorbidity consultation:
It's rare enough in my experience that a patient will come and say that my only problem today is knee pain.
GP Stakeholder 6

In response, a checklist embedded in the physiotherapy referral form (Prompts/cues) would cue GPs to complete elements of the enhanced consultation, e.g., provide Patient Advice Leaflet. The checklist would also provide repeated reinforcement of desirable behaviours, and successful implementation interventions from low back pain research suggest that at least one component of an implementation intervention should be ongoing over time [98].

Physiotherapist stakeholders supported the initiation of exercise prescription by GPs, noting that it would provide useful preliminary information on patients' responses to exercise. As part of their ‘enhanced consultation’, GPs would refer patients to an early ‘best practice’ physiotherapy session (Restructuring the social environment) for tailored advice, exercise prescription and a self‐management plan. The use of a single physiotherapy session was supported by evidence from other chronic musculoskeletal conditions. A robust single session had comparable results for pain, function and quality of life when compared to multiple physiotherapy sessions [99, 100]. To optimise the acceptability of a single session, PwLE stakeholders suggested including access to follow‐up advice over the telephone, where additional guidance was required.

Several self‐regulatory BCTs, which have been shown to boost self‐efficacy and exercise adherence, were integrated into the ‘best practice’ physiotherapy session (Goal setting [outcome], action planning, self‐monitoring of behaviour, behavioural practice/rehearsal, and adding objects to the environment) [101, 102, 103]. There was unanimous support from PwLE for the provision of resources and practical strategies to support self‐management (knowledge and skills and verbal persuasion about capability). One stakeholder commented:
I think it's only when the emphasis is put on your own participation in your recovery and in plain simple terms you are told, “You have to do this. and here's how you are going to do it.”
PwLE Stakeholder 4

Physiotherapist stakeholders emphasised the need for a longer session to facilitate the delivery of individualised education and allow time to explore beliefs and expectations related to symptoms and exercise (reduce negative emotions, re‐attribution, framing/reframing and verbal persuasion about capability). Training and resources to support the delivery of this single session were also considered important by physiotherapist stakeholders. Stakeholders viewed consistency of messaging between the GP and the physiotherapist as vital to support deferral of imaging and optimise patient engagement with a self‐management approach (Social support [unspecified] and information about others' approval).

Intervention components that required substantial organisational support or change were excluded due to the feasibility of future scale‐up. This included suggestions from stakeholders such as the provision of a specialist knee interface clinic for GPs, offering free access to physiotherapy within GP practices, and access to publicly funded personal trainers. Timely access to physiotherapy was identified as key to providing evidence‐based care; however, waiting times of 4–12 months within the public health service represented a substantial barrier. To overcome this, we negotiated with local physiotherapy management to enable access within 2–3 weeks to a 1‐h physiotherapy session (restructuring physical environment). Accessing this early session will promote GP engagement with the intervention and will not disqualify patients from accessing further physiotherapy outside this intervention, should they so choose.

The final selected BCTs, including content and mode of delivery, mapped to TDF domains and barriers are shown in Tables 2 and 3. Several additional elements, which did not map to specific barriers, were incorporated to enhance intervention implementation and GP engagement.
For training purposes, GP stakeholders specified a preference for workshops to be incentivised with Continuing Professional Development credits (self‐incentive).

Social influences are important in clinical practice, and interventions to change social norms can be effective in changing the clinical behaviours [104]; therefore, GPs who are influential amongst their peers (GP tutor × 1, clinical academic GP × 1 and GP leads of trainee scheme × 1) will be purposively invited to attend these small group workshops to leverage their social influence.

The final intervention was based on what was likely to be feasible, acceptable and relevant locally. It consisted of small group educational workshops targeted at GPs and the provision of GP educational resources to facilitate delivery of an ‘enhanced consultation’ to patients. GPs had the facility to refer patients to an early ‘best practice’ physiotherapy session. The patient‐targeted intervention had two main steps: an ‘enhanced consultation’ with the GP, followed by a ‘best practice’ physiotherapy session. An overview of the final intervention with rationale for inclusion of the intervention components based on APEASE criteria is presented in Table 4. The Patient Advice Leaflet was modified to incorporate feedback from stakeholders. This is mainly related to the accessibility of the language, and PwLE stakeholders also recommended highlighting the evidence proving arthroscopy was not more effective than sham surgery. GP stakeholders recommended that an electronic version of the resource should be made available.

sections.title: Step 4: How Can Behaviour Change Be Measured and Understood?

paragraphs.en: The intervention aims to facilitate healthcare professional and patient behaviour change. Behavioural analysis indicated that GPs require greater confidence, knowledge and skills to modify clinical practice. Training workshops will enhance self‐efficacy in musculoskeletal assessment, patient education and exercise prescription, while increasing motivation to adopt evidence‐based care and reduce unnecessary imaging and specialist referral. Communication training and practical strategies to manage patient expectations are expected to further reduce referrals, with the physical examination promoted as a means of reassurance and reframing pain, rather than solely a diagnostic task. Early access to physiotherapy will address organisational barriers to optimal care.

Patient behaviour change is expected through interactions with both GPs and physiotherapists. GPs will foster positive recovery expectations through an enhanced consultation and facilitate access to evidence‐based physiotherapy. Both professionals will work to modify beliefs about exercise and surgery and enhance self‐efficacy by providing support and guidance for self‐management and increased physical activity.

A logic model (Figure 2) of the GP and patient‐level interventions, mapped to hypothesised mechanisms of change and outcomes, was developed. We also outlined outcomes designed to capture change in GP and patient behaviour for measurement in a feasibility study (Table 5).

This study describes the systematic development of a multi‐level, theory‐informed implementation intervention designed to improve evidence‐based management of DMT and early knee OA. By integrating behavioural theory, stakeholder input and empirical evidence, our intervention directly addresses well‐documented evidence–practice gaps in the conservative management of degenerative knee conditions.

Through its explicit focus on early‐stage disease, this work addresses an important gap in the OA literature. To our knowledge, it is the first intervention designed to specifically target patients with DMT and early OA, a group often funnelled prematurely towards imaging and surgical consultation, having bypassed the core treatments of education and exercise. To date, much of the research involving patients with DMT has focused on comparing the effectiveness of non‐surgical approaches to arthroscopic surgery [29, 105, 106]. The current study takes the next logical step, which is to focus on implementing this evidence by designing an intervention to address the real‐world barriers to both the delivery and uptake of exercise and education for this patient cohort with early degenerative changes [36, 51]. A related implementation approach was taken in the UK National Health Service through the Personalised Knee Improvement Programme (P‐KIP), which was developed specifically to address behavioural and service‐level barriers to reducing arthroscopy for knee OA [107] and provide an evidence‐based conservative care pathway as an alternative. However, P‐KIP sought to substitute conservative care (education, physiotherapy and dietetic support) for arthroscopy, once patients with established knee OA had reached secondary care [108]. Meanwhile, the current intervention targets an earlier point in the care pathway by supporting evidence‐based management at the primary care consultation, before patients progress to imaging and specialist referral. Nonetheless, P‐KIP provides a useful real‐world example of de‐implementing arthroscopy, and its service evaluation illustrates the potential value of providing clinicians with a ‘substitute’ pathway to established low‐value care pathways. Our intervention adopts a similar approach and attempts to provide GPs with a credible alternative, via the provision of educational resources for patients and early access to a ‘best practice’ physiotherapy session, rather than focusing solely on reducing inappropriate clinical behaviours related to imaging and early referral to secondary care.

The behavioural analysis underpinning our intervention highlights that the evidence practice gaps are not driven by lack of knowledge alone, but by complex interactions between clinician beliefs and confidence, patient expectations, social norms, and system‐level constraints. These findings are consistent with prior work suggesting that implementing evidence‐based care for OA is a complex behavioural and organisational problem, not simply an information problem [45, 58, 69, 109]. A recently published evidence synthesis of barriers and enablers to the implementation of primary care‐based OA management programmes highlights the importance of the health system environment, with over one‐third of barriers and enablers relating to the broader health system [45]. Difficulty accessing care in the public sector, long delays, workforce shortages and patients being prematurely waitlisted are challenges to the provision of high‐quality OA care, both in Ireland and internationally [58, 110]. Health system capacity and resources were also cited as prominent barriers to evidence‐based care for early OA and DMTs in our study. This implies that implementation cannot rely solely on changing GP and patient behaviour, and the feasibility of scaling up this intervention will also depend on sufficient physiotherapy capacity to provide timely access to evidence‐based care. In Ireland, there is a critical need to build workforce capacity and ensure adequate resourcing of primary care physiotherapy [111]. Addressing these health system and service barriers requires health system and policy reform, including financing models that better support and incentivise high‐value OA care [110]. Future development work should also include policy‐makers to prioritise the implementation of current OA models of care into practice.

Another important barrier identified in our needs analysis, but considered broadly beyond the scope of the current study, was societal narratives and unhelpful beliefs about a predominantly structural model of musculoskeletal pain. Patient beliefs about the need for surgery and imaging were reinforced by their wider social circle. Such beliefs are recognised to contribute to low‐value care by shaping people's expectations of care and how they interact with clinicians [112, 113]. Comprehensively addressing these population‐level beliefs and promoting a narrative that supports active self‐management and physical activity necessitates public health campaigns to provide a broader re‐framing of musculoskeletal pain in society [114].

A major strength of this study is the extensive stakeholder engagement across PwLE, GPs, physiotherapists and orthopaedic surgeons. We specifically chose the four‐step design approach by French et al. as it allows for the integration of stakeholder perspectives [59]. Stakeholder involvement is increasingly recognised as essential for enhancing intervention acceptability and feasibility, particularly for complex interventions implemented in real‐world healthcare settings [67, 68]. Stakeholder feedback meaningfully shaped target behaviours, intervention components and modes of delivery, thereby increasing the likelihood of successful implementation. For the purposes of conducting this stakeholder engagement, we chose to meet with groups of stakeholders separately. This decision was driven by evidence suggesting this approach is more acceptable and useful to stakeholders, who can feel their opinion is undervalued in a mixed group of HCPs and patients, compared to combining multiple stakeholders in a single group [115]. Nonetheless, this approach is more time‐consuming, involving multiple meetings, six in this study, with additional stakeholder engagement via email. The use of the widely used TDF framework to identify modifiable behavioural determinants strengthens the rigour and transparency of the intervention design process. Explicitly naming the hypothesised mechanisms of change means they can be specifically tested in future investigations.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. Firstly, qualitative data underpinning the behavioural analysis and stakeholder input were drawn from a single healthcare region. Specific local contextual factors may limit transferability to other healthcare settings with different funding, infrastructure and access. Furthermore, the use of existing qualitative datasets, while focused on the target cohort (people with DMT or early OA), meant the analysis was limited to issues explored within the original interviews. Secondly, while broad stakeholder perspectives were sought, a formal consensus methodology such as a Delphi process was not employed. Thirdly, organisational barriers such as long physiotherapy waiting lists were mitigated pragmatically through discussions with local health service management, rather than addressing this problem at a systems level, which may affect the potential to scale up the intervention. Fourthly, this intervention focused on education and exercise. Weight management is another key aspect of knee OA care. While this was covered in the GP education workshop, we did not have the resources to facilitate access to individualised weight management support. This aspect of care is arguably even more important for individuals with early OA, given that future weight gain and adiposity drive disease progression [116]. Finally, empirical evidence to prove theory‐driven interventions demonstrate greater effectiveness in changing professional behaviour is still sparse [117], as is the evidence to support their effectiveness for superior clinical outcomes [51]; therefore, testing of this intervention in practice is key. Until this, its acceptability, fidelity and effectiveness remain uncertain.

sections.title: Implications for Policy, Practice and Future Research

paragraphs.en: In terms of clinical implications, if this intervention is feasible and effective, it has the potential to reduce low‐value imaging and surgical referral, promote earlier engagement with self‐management, and improve patient confidence in conservative care. Embedding early consistent, evidence‐based messages at the patient–practitioner interface may also reduce fear‐driven healthcare utilisation and support more sustainable models of musculoskeletal care. Given the growing burden of OA disease and its associated comorbidities, this intervention aligns with a new focus on secondary prevention of early knee OA [118]. This intervention provides a structured example of intervening early, providing patients with a tailored plan and potentially influencing the subsequent disease process.

The next stage of this project will be a feasibility study to help address outstanding uncertainties in relation to the intervention. It is important to understand if the ‘enhanced GP consultation’ and the ‘best practice’ physiotherapy session are acceptable to patients and HCPs and feasible to deliver within the Irish public healthcare system. A mixed‐methods approach will be used, including qualitative interviews with patients and GPs to explore experiences of the intervention, perceived usefulness, and barriers and facilitators to participation and delivery. Acceptability will be assessed using the Theoretical Framework of Acceptability (TFA) questionnaire [119], while satisfaction with care will be measured using a self‐rated ordinal scale. Potential behavioural outcomes include changes in GP management practices, such as imaging and secondary care referrals and patient engagement with recommended self‐management strategies. Feasibility will additionally be assessed through recruitment and retention rates for GPs and patients, providing an indication of the ability to engage and retain patients attending primary care as study participants. Findings will inform further refinement of the intervention and the feasibility of progressing to a full trial. Finally, a feasibility study will also provide an opportunity to further test and refine educational materials for patients and HCPs. For example, ensuring the accessibility of the Patient Advice Leaflet is an important consideration, including a formal assessment of readability, colour contrast and digital accessibility, or potentially developing alternative formats such as large‐print, audio or Easy Read versions to ensure equitable access across diverse patient groups.

Using a systematic, theory‐informed and stakeholder‐engaged approach, we developed a multifaceted intervention to support delivery and uptake of evidence‐based care for DMT and early knee OA. The intervention comprised small‐group educational workshops and resources for GPs to support the delivery of an ‘enhanced consultation’, with the facility to refer patients for an early ‘best practice’ physiotherapy session. The patient intervention, therefore, consisted of two key components: an ‘enhanced consultation’ with the GP followed by a ‘best practice’ physiotherapy session. This single session delivers individualised education and a bespoke exercise and physical activity plan to boost self‐management and self‐efficacy. The resulting intervention requires testing to explore its acceptability, feasibility and suitability for scale‐up in clinical practice.

tables.caption: Summary of final intervention components with rationale for inclusion based on APEASE criteria.
rows: Intervention component and mode of delivery
Rationale for inclusion based on research team consideration of the APEASE * criteria
GP level

Interactive small group workshops (accredited with GP CPD points) delivered by experienced MSK physiotherapists. Workshops include: (i) update on evidence (use of exercise v's surgery, weight management, imaging indications, practice guidelines for DMT/early OA), (ii) conducting focused knee exam (red flags, differential diagnosis), (iii) communication tips and navigating discussion around need for imaging and (iv) delivering components of GP's ‘enhanced consultation’

Interactive workshops have demonstrated effectiveness (as part of multi‐component strategies); acceptable to GP stakeholders; affordable and practicable to deliver within the scope of the current project
GP level

Provision of GP resources (hard and digital copies) to support consultation including: (i) a quick reference guide to aid diagnosis, (ii) a quick reference guide on key aspects of management and ‘enhanced consultation’, (iii) a Patient Advice Leaflet and (iv) exercise prescription resources.
Affordable and practicable to deliver within the scope of the current project; acceptable to GP stakeholders
GP level
Self‐complete checklist on components of GP's ‘enhanced consultation’ embedded into physiotherapy referral form
Checklist practicable for GPs to complete as part of the physiotherapy referral process; acceptable to GP stakeholders
GP level
Written feedback to GP via physiotherapist discharge summary (re‐enforcing accuracy of GPs' clinical diagnosis and patient suitability for conservative management)

Practicable and affordable means of delivering feedback and reinforcing GP behaviour. Physiotherapist discharge summary is already part of routine care; acceptable to GP and physiotherapist stakeholders
GP level
Facility to refer patients to an early ‘Best Practice’ physiotherapy session (appointment within 2–3 weeks of GP consultation)
Demonstrates equity as all patients are entitled to access*; acceptable to all stakeholders
Patient level

GP ‘enhanced consultation’ to include: (i) clinical knee exam, (ii) verbally delivered educational messages, (iii) Patient Advice Leaflet and (iv) management plan agreed and documented on Patient Advice Leaflet

Individual components of consultation acceptable to GP and PwLE stakeholders; GP's ‘model consultations’ have previously demonstrated effectiveness; delivery mode deemed practicable as it fits within existing GP practice; no side effects or safety issues identified with delaying referral (restricting GPs' ability to refer for non‐indicated imaging may have presented safety issues)
Patient level

Patient Advice Leaflet designed to reassure and explain diagnosis, reinforce verbally delivered educational messages and help guide pain monitoring during activity. Section for co‐creating a treatment plan, simple starter exercises with progressions and QR codes linking to exercise videos
Component is practicable and affordable; acceptable to GP and PwLE stakeholders
Patient level

Physiotherapy ‘Best Practice’ session encompassing: (i) individualised patient education on likely prognosis, beliefs about pain, physical activity, weight management and other lifestyle factors; (ii) education on self‐management skills such as load management, activity modification and monitoring pain response; (iii) functional or physical activity goals identified and action plan created; (iv) introduction of logbook to self‐monitor physical activity and (v) graded exercise programme linked to functional goals, practised with physio, with options to progress and regress exercises

A similar single session approach has demonstrated effectiveness and is practicable to deliver; acceptable to GP, PwLE and physiotherapist stakeholders; no side effects or safety issues identified; demonstrates equity as all patients are entitled to access**
